📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whey protein powder is a popular supplement because it’s a simple and effective way to increase daily protein intake.

Whey is a complete protein that contains all nine essential amino acids our bodies need to build muscle. Whey protein also supplies the body with branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), like leucine, which help promote muscle growth (1).

We consulted Pete Nastasi, a certified nutrition coach (C.N.C.), to help us find the best whey protein powders on the market.

Industry observers note that here, we break down the different types of whey protein powders available (concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate), which types will work best for you, and what nutrition information to look for. Plus, we’ve tested over 50 protein powders to help us create the list of our top picks.

Medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

Recent findings suggest that we chose products for our list of the best whey protein powders based on a number of factors reflected in our whey protein powder scoring methodology. These include:.

We also receive input from our panel of expert contributors, which includes registered dietitians and highly credentialed experts in sports nutrition and exercise science.

No sugar, all protein—that’s what Transparent Labs set out to accomplish with its grass-fed whey protein isolate. This whey protein undergoes filtration (2), taking out the excess sugar, fat, carbs, and lactose so you’re giving your body the pure protein it needs to rebuild. Whey isolate has the highest protein concentration of the different types of protein powders, and this protein is a good option if you’re trying to reduce your carb and fat intake.

Transparent Labs’ Whey Protein Isolate packs 28 grams of protein into each serving—one of the highest on our list. We also like the flavor variety, including unique flavors like Cinnamon French Toast. Bonus: This protein isn’t too sweet, so you can mix it with fruit juice or add it to a fruit smoothie without feeling like you’re drinking a shake made with Fun Dip.

Sports Research Whey Protein is formulated with 6.9 grams of BCAAs, including 1,000 milligrams of L-leucine. Studies show leucine may help reduce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). Depending on flavor, this Informed Sport Certified protein powder is sweetened with stevia or sucralose, so those sensitive to these ingredients may need to steer clear.

In a recent development, rachel Pasche indicates she has a protein shake for dessert some nights using the Dutch Chocolate flavor. “It might be too sweet for some people, but I honestly love the taste so much,” she says. “It’s my favorite flavor of protein powder I’ve ever tried.” She says the powder mixes well with water alone, with both a handheld mixer and in a shaker cup, noting there is some foam at the top that doesn’t last long and no clumping.

Additionally, Pasche claims she sometimes feels bloated after whey protein shakes, but after six months of using Sports Research Whey, she has not experienced any bloat.

Recent findings suggest that why is grass-fed whey protein better? Studies show that dairy sourced from grass-fed cows has a higher concentration of whey proteins and amino acids (3), which may further support muscular training adaptations.

This Nutricost protein powder is non-GMO, gluten-free, and third-party tested. Whey protein concentrate, like this one, is often made with sunflower lecithin, an ingredient to help promote mixability. Testers also enjoy the taste and say this protein powder mixes well. “The taste was nostalgic; I’d liken it to Nesquik,” says tester Grant Smith. “And the mixability was on par with some of the better proteins I’ve had previously.” Smith was pleasantly surprised by the mixability of Nutricost Whey Protein, noting he didn’t find any small chunks of undissolved protein floating in his shake when mixed with milk.

After drinking most of his shake, Smith let a bit of the mixture sit for almost 10 minutes after initially mixing to test for separation. He noticed some slight separation between the protein and skim milk he mixed it with, but says it wasn’t enough to make the drink any less appealing.

The protein in Legion Athletics is certified to contain no banned substances by Labdoor, the gold standard of third-party lab testing. This helps ensure the protein isolate is in its purest, most nutritionally dense form without any interference from pesticides and growth hormones.

Additionally, Legion Athletics whey is filtered to remove extra carbs and fat, so you’re only getting the good stuff with every serving. The removal of these elements is geared toward bloat-free digestion.

According to recent reports, testers say it also tastes great, giving especially high marks to the French Vanilla flavor. “I really like the flavor of this one. It tastes like a vanilla creamer!” indicates Kayla Godfrey. “This is delicious. Great vanilla taste,” says Carlo Barajas.

You’ve probably seen that one of the biggest general complaints about protein powder is it can taste “chalky” and leave you with an off-putting aftertaste. Our testing team tried Gainful’s Caffe Mocha flavor, and liked the subtle, not-too-sweet flavor profile. “This reminds me of an at-home cappuccino mix,” says Barry Bridges. “The coffee flavor is very light—I’d say it’s more of a chocolate flavor,” adds Rachael Harris.

If you’re not a fan of coffee flavors, Gainful offers nine total flavors in individual-use packets, so you can pick and choose what you’re craving each day. Nastasi, who has tried many different Gainful Protein Powder flavors, says the Chocolate Peanut Butter, Caffe Mocha, and Sea Salt Caramel are his favorites.

Whey protein is a concentrated protein source derived from cow’s milk, which contains two major proteins called casein and whey (4). Whey accounts for 20 percent of milk protein, and is considered a high-quality protein source. Cow’s milk protein is considered a complete protein because it contains all nine essential amino acids required by the body (5).

Beyond basic nutrition, whey protein (6) may offer specific health benefits, such as enhanced immune function (7) and cardiometabolic health (8). Usually, whey is sold in powder form, which can be blended with water or other liquids or added to soft foods. Also, people use whey protein powder in cooking, which adds nutritional value to baked goods. Food manufacturers use whey formulations rather than cream, butter, or egg ingredients to make high-protein, low-fat products.

Sources indicate that when you browse online or at your local nutrition shop for whey protein products, you’ll probably notice different forms of whey. The main difference in the types of whey protein is how they’re processed. The three most common forms of whey protein are concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate (hydrolyzed whey).

Whey protein concentrate (WPC) is the least processed form of whey, so it contains the highest levels of lactose (milk sugar), fat, carbohydrates, and nutrients. Food manufacturers use WPC (9) to replace fresh dairy and eggs in products like sauces, soups, and baked goods because it adds flavor, color, and texture and extends shelf-life (10). However, it has the lowest protein content out of the three—typically 70 to 80 percent.

In a recent development, whey protein isolate (WPI) is made when whey is filtered and processed. It contains the most protein, 90 percent or more, and less lactose. Because of its higher protein content, sports nutrition companies often prefer WPI for use in supplements, protein bars, and other protein products (11). However, it lacks some of the beneficial nutrients found in the concentrated form (12).

In a recent development, whey protein hydrolysate (WPH), also known as hydrolyzed whey, is produced by a process called partial hydrolysis, which breaks down whey protein for easier absorption (13). WPH is digested faster than WPC or WPI (14), so it causes a 28 to 43 percent increase in blood sugar levels (15). Diabetics don’t have to worry about this, though. Protein digestion is slow. In fact, recent research suggests that whey protein improves glycemic (blood sugar) control (16).

Industry observers note that the real benefit of a whey protein powder is that it’s an incredibly convenient and high-quality source of dietary protein. However, if you consume enough dietary protein through meat, dairy, legumes, and other foods, then you don’t need a protein powder to achieve your health and fitness goals. However, if you’re having trouble consuming enough protein through your diet alone, then adding a protein powder to your daily routine can have some real benefits.

It has been revealed that whey protein is rich in essential amino acids, including BCAAs, which can be beneficial for supporting muscle integrity and growth with training (17). Adding a protein powder for muscle gain to your daily diet can be a great way to help maximize your dietary protein intake and stimulate muscle growth.

When you’re in a caloric deficit with the goal of losing weight, you want to ensure that the weight you’re losing is primarily fat and not muscle. Eating a diet rich in protein helps preserve the lean muscle mass you’ve worked hard to achieve and enables your body to prioritize burning fat for energy.

Consuming whey protein has a satiating effect, meaning that it helps you feel full for a longer period of time. High protein diets help with weight loss by regulating your hunger levels and therefore reducing the amount of total calories you consume throughout the day.

In order to properly use a whey protein powder, you should first determine how much protein you should be eating on a daily basis. The amount of protein you consume is dependent on your fitness goals and current body weight, activity level, and physique. A simple way to calculate your daily protein intake is by multiplying your body weight by 0.8. The resulting number is how many grams of protein you should consume each day. This should provide most active individuals with sufficient protein intake. Remember that whey protein powder is a supplement and shouldn’t be your main source of dietary protein.

As far as how to consume this protein powder, you should follow the instructions on the supplement label. This usually entails mixing one scoop of protein powder with 10 to 12 ounces of your favorite beverage. It can also be mixed in a smoothie or foods like oatmeal and pancake batter. Whey protein powder can be consumed at any time of the day, but it’s usually utilized as a post-workout supplement to begin repairing muscle tissue.

Industry observers note that when used in moderation, protein powder is free of side effects and generally considered safe for healthy adults. However, consuming large amounts of protein powder can lead to digestive problems, dehydration, and (potentially) nutrient deficiencies. It’s important to use whey protein powder as part of a balanced diet and not as your main source of dietary protein. If you experience any unusual symptoms after using protein powder, stop use immediately and consult a healthcare professional.

A whey protein powder will benefit anyone who is looking to increase their daily protein consumption and has trouble doing so through their diet alone. This is especially relevant for very active individuals, such as athletes, bodybuilders, and fitness enthusiasts who have increased protein demands due to their workouts and training.

Another segment of the population that may benefit from using a whey protein powder is older adults. As we age, our bodies become less efficient at absorbing protein from food (18). Using protein supplements can be an easy way for older adults to meet their daily protein needs and support muscle health.

When picking a whey protein product, there are a few factors to consider, including the type of protein, taste, nutrition, additives/allergies, and price.

Check the ingredients list to see what type of whey the protein powder contains. Some brands will use a blend of whey forms.

Recent findings suggest that whey proteins come in a wide variety of flavors. You’ll find options from unflavored to vanilla, chocolate orange, and summer berries, to name a few. Taste is key because you want a protein supplement you’ll enjoy. When just starting to supplement your protein intake, try a small container or buy samples of flavors you might enjoy and get creative with your add-ins. You can try fruits, flavored milks, or juices to create new flavors that fit your taste preference.

It has been revealed that check the whey protein label for the amount of protein per serving, and factor it into your daily protein intake. Most protein powders have around 25 grams per serving, which is an ideal dosage to maximize muscle protein synthesis (19). Also look for calories, fats, carbs, fiber, vitamins, and minerals and even amino acid profiles. Make sure that the supplement you choose gives you the maximum benefit without unnecessary add-ins.

According to recent reports, read the ingredients section, too. Look for additives or allergens that you want or need to avoid. For example, labels warn you if the whey powder contains soy or was processed in a facility with nuts.

The protein powders on our list give you a good idea of the price range for whey supplements. Our top picks vary from $1.16 to $3.41 per serving or $34 to $95 per container, so there’s an option for most budgets.

In a recent development, it depends on your body’s unique needs and health and fitness goals. You should include protein with meals or snacks every three to five hours (20), but no one should rely solely on protein powder because that would eliminate other nutritious whole foods from the diet.One whey protein drink per day is reasonable. Check with your doctor if you want to use whey protein to replace more than one meal.

Yes, whey protein powder is generally considered safe for healthy individuals when used in moderation. If you have any pre-existing medical conditions or have a severe lactose intolerance, consult with a healthcare professional before adding a whey protein powder to your diet.

According to recent reports, there really is no “best time” to take a whey protein powder supplement. Instead, your timing depends on your individual goals and lifestyle. Some people enjoy a protein shake in the morning as a quick and easy breakfast option they can have on the go, while others prefer to consume it immediately after a workout to support muscle growth and recovery.Just remember that whey protein powder should be used as a supplement to a well-balanced diet, and should not be used as a replacement for whole nutrient-dense foods. The timing of when you consume the whey protein is less crucial than your overall protein intake throughout the day.

Recent findings suggest that from keeping you satiated to helping you improve your performance in the gym, whey protein powder can certainly help you lose weight. Research has even shown that whey protein may reduce abdominal fat when combined with weight training (21).

If overused, whey protein can cause side effects (22), including kidney or liver damage, aggression, acne, and a disruption in gut bacteria. Since most people don’t consume more than one serving of whey protein per day, overconsumption is rare and takes time to develop. If you would like to add an extra layer of protection for your gut bacteria, you can even take a high-quality prebiotic or ensure you consume a variety of fruits and vegetables on a regular basis.

Industry observers note that the best way to know if your whey protein is high quality is to read the labels. Check out the whey source, nutritional profile, and ingredient list. Quality wheys use traceable, organic, and certified ingredients. Also, high-quality whey products avoid fillers and artificial sweeteners. Another sign that you have a good quality whey is when the labels include certifications and seals from third-party approvals. These show that the manufacturer has proven the quality by established standards.

I Thought I Was Getting Slower Because of Age. Then an Incidental Scan Revealed the Real Problem—and Likely Saved My Life.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last year, a lung scan—ordered even though I’d ground out my last butt decades earlier—incidentally picked up a bulge in my aorta.
  • I was in my mid-fifties and healthy.
  • Further tests revealed the diameter of my aorta to be twice the normal size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smoking may have saved my life.

Recent findings suggest that last year, a lung scan—ordered even though I’d ground out my last butt decades earlier—incidentally picked up a bulge in my aorta. Because I smoked heavily when I was young, my doctor sent me for a screening after the age eligibility had been lowered, just in case. While the scan didn’t find any signs of cancer, it detected something else. An aneurysm: a weak spot in the body’s main artery that causes it to balloon.

I was baffled. I was in my mid-fifties and healthy. I had no family history of cardiovascular problems. I was a longtime runner. I ate my veggies and hadn’t had a drink in 27 years. My resting heart rate was borderline smug.

Further tests revealed the diameter of my aorta to be twice the normal size. Putting me at risk of an aortic dissection or rupture, both life-threatening emergencies that demand immediate treatment.

Sources indicate that damn. How long had I been walking—and running—around with this fault line trembling in my chest?

While waiting for an appointment with a cardiologist, I was seized with anxiety. I stopped exercising. I practiced randomly unlocking the emergency feature on my phone and quickly making a mental note of my location.

An echocardiogram later revealed that the bulge had also pulled apart the leaflets of my aortic valve, preventing them from sealing tightly. With every heartbeat, some of the blood my heart pumped out leaked backward, forcing it to work harder to circulate the same blood twice.

“Given that you’re only in your fifties and live an active lifestyle,” the cardiologist said, “I’d suggest you consult with a cardiac surgeon.”.

The last sentence I thought I’d ever hear. Until I was met with, “Let’s schedule you for open-heart surgery.”.

In a recent development, looking back, I wondered if there had been signs. I had tried to run at least one marathon or ultra a year, along with some shorter distances. In recent years, no matter how hard I trained, I could never improve my times, my marathons creeping up from low four hours to a whisper below five. I increasingly had to run/walk the final miles. I tried a vegan diet to improve my energy and switched to forefoot running for more spring in my stride. Nothing budged. Maybe I was just getting older.

In a recent development, gradually, and then seemingly all at once, running became a grind. I started cutting workouts short. The hills felt steeper. The part I looked forward to most was stopping. The joy I had always found in movement was supplanted by fatigue and frustration and more frequent visits to my physical therapist. After plodding across the finish line at the 2025 Falmouth Road Race, I hit the pause button and wondered if I’d ever press play again.

Running has been part of my identity for most of my adult life. After years of flailing, it demonstrated me I was capable. It soothed the anxieties of sobriety and helped me believe I was more than the drunken jerk many people knew when I was in my teens and twenties. It was a sandbox for role-playing difficult conversations, reckoning with my trespasses, and cultivating humility. It was where the idea for my first book took shape and stories took root. It was a way to find people like me, if only through those knowing waves as we passed. Running was more than a healthy habit. It was a partner, my better half.

In a recent development, after all these years, had I fallen out of love? And if I had, who would I be without it?

Industry observers note that open-heart surgery involves slicing through the chest, sawing the sternum in two, parting the halves with a retractor, and stopping the heart. The task of keeping you alive is outsourced to a machine. Even though doctors have been successfully performing this procedure for decades, when it’s you going up on that table, it feels like science fiction.

Sources indicate that as the date of my surgery crept closer, fear and anxiety filled me like a helium balloon. The idea of intubation kept me up at night. What if I wake gagging and rip the tube out?

The mortality rate was one in a hundred.

Sources indicate that I calmed myself the way I would before a significant race: meditation, yoga, and Peggy Huddleston’s pre-surgery relaxation techniques. I studied “the course” and sought out people who’d been through it, looking for any kind of mental edge. And though I was not a religious person, I asked friends and family for prayers, having read that they’d been shown to influence outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that early one morning in February, I was wheeled into an operating bay at Massachusetts General Hospital, knocked unconscious and chemically paralyzed. Over the next five hours, my surgeon removed my diseased aortic root and ascending aorta, replaced them with a synthetic graft and carbon valve, and hooked my coronary arteries back up to the new plumbing.

When they took me off bypass, my heart forgot how to beat. Instead of pumping, it quivered, seized by electrical chaos. Ventricular fibrillation. The doctors had to shock my heart back into rhythm. Four times. Inside the cardiac OR, the team was ready. Anywhere else, it would have been goodnight, Irene.

In a recent development, I knew none of this when I groggily opened my eyes in the ICU that evening. I felt trampled. I could see the breathing tube that had haunted me for weeks protruding from my mouth, my hands bound to the bedrail to keep me from reaching for it, but I felt no urge, couldn’t feel it. The second time I woke up—the first just brief enough to realize where I was—a voice said, “Squeeze my hand.” My eyelids too heavy to lift, I managed, then drifted back into blackness. When I stirred again, the tube was gone. Relief. But drainage lines snaked from my chest into canisters, while wires and catheters tethered me to a forest of blinking monitors.

Later, in the step-down cardiac ward, I needed a walker to cover even the shortest distance, the drainage boxes hanging on the sides like hard saddlebags. I was carrying 15 extra pounds of fluid, my fingers fat as cocktail wieners. I shuffled down the hall in grippy socks, a tech beside me and a chair trailing behind should I need to sit.

I spent a week at Mass General, three months of recovery ahead of me. In the early weeks, the focus was on walking. Three minutes at a time. Twice a day. Getting to the end of the block took effort. My wife (stone-cold angel!) set up chairs on the landing so I could stop and catch my breath going upstairs in our house outside of Boston. Instead of crushing miles, I was crushing naps.

At six weeks, I met with my surgeon for a follow-up. She was pleased with my progress and lifted some restrictions and cleared me for cardiac rehab. She showed me a picture of my valve leaflets riddled with holes. Told me the aneurysm had likely been there for a decade, the aortic wall “paper thin.” I felt dizzy as if peering over the edge of a tall building. You hear about runners collapsing at the end of marathons, about shovelers going down after a snowstorm. Had it only been a matter of time?

As she described the repair—a Bentall procedure, one of the more complex operations in cardiac surgery—a seductive thought wormed its way into my brain. Sure, aging may have started to slow me down, but a leaky, punctured valve must have been robbing my body of strength and energy, too. Now that a set of brand-latest carbon leaflets was opening and closing tightly, blood safely moving in the right direction, could I get my running back on track? Maybe emerge stronger and faster, start breaking PRs again. Could I fall back in love?

I stared at my surgeon, the woman who had held my heart in her hands. Had she seen that old spark still flickering in there?

Industry observers note that cardiac rehab is part safety net, part exercise boot camp. A mini gym with EKG leads and blood-pressure cuffs. When I walked in, an elderly woman in jeans pedaled a recumbent bike while a silver-haired man in a rugby shirt and mask worked an arm cycle. Nearby, an old man plucked one of the resistance ropes that hung from hooks like a swarm of eels. Not everyone had undergone surgery. Some were recovering from heart attacks or stent procedures, others from dangerous arrhythmias or heart failure. I didn’t see anyone else my age.

A physical therapist named Andi asked about my surgery and fitness history, then my goals.

“The seven-mile Falmouth Road Race in four months,” I stated. Returning a year later, with a sternum fused by wire, felt like a symbolic milestone. For good measure, I added, “and a marathon next spring.”.

According to recent reports, I leaned back, waiting for her eyes to light up with amazement. I bet she didn’t hear that very often. She kept scribbling. Probably too stunned, I figured.

She handed me a laminated workout card. “No treadmill?” I frowned. “Soon. Let’s see how you do with these exercises.”.

I climbed onto a stationary bike and quietly turned the resistance a few notches above the prescribed setting. I watched my heart rate climb on the monitor above the nurse’s station: 100, 110, 120. Sweat prickled my forehead. That old feeling. For almost two months, my body had belonged to surgeons, nurses, and restrictions. Now, little by little, it would be returned to its rightful owner.

Recent findings suggest that andi kept her promise. A few weeks later, she prescribed one minute of running. Sixty seconds at a 14-minute pace, followed by two minutes of walking. Five intervals. Three-quarters of a mile. The longest I’d run in eight months. It felt every bit as satisfying as finishing a marathon.

As I built from one-minute intervals to two, then three, I stopped thinking so much about future PRs and training plans. I was running again. The minutes stretched. The walks grew shorter. The weeks passed. By the third month, I was running two miles continuously and sweating so much that the EKG leads kept popping off my chest. Andi would laugh and hand me a fresh set.

When I arrived, I’d seen those sticky leads as signs that I was still a patient. Now they wouldn’t stay on, blanking out my little section on the wall monitor.

Sources indicate that on August 16, 2026, I stood among the heaving throngs on Water Street in Woods Hole, the staging area for the Falmouth Road Race on Cape Cod. I stroked my chest. Still tender six months later. Amid shouts and laughter, selfies and the sharp medicinal smell of Bengay mixed with sunscreen, my mind hummed with questions: Was I still the runner I used to be? Did we have a future together? Had my slump been caused by my heart—or “my heart?”.

Every few minutes, the crowd surged forward, then stopped, then surged again—an electrical current passing through thousands of bodies as waves of runners were slowly released onto the course.

Industry observers note that at last we crossed the starting line. As I set off, an old familiar voice rose to taunt me: This doesn’t count as your substantial comeback if you take walk breaks, and Dave McGillivray ran the entire Boston Marathon six months after heart surgery.

Industry observers note that but then the race gave me something else to listen to. The pounding of rubber soles like golf applause. Spectators shaking cowbells and waving signs. The theme song from “Rocky” pouring from unseen speakers at Nobska Light. The cheers rose around us, and somewhere beyond them the waters of Vineyard Sound flashed in the sun, the island a squiggle on the horizon. Then an emptiness settled over the salty air.

Sources indicate that I found myself thinking about who I had become. Or maybe who I’d spent my adult life trying to become. The abstinent runner. The marathoner chasing his father’s PR. The ultrarunner. The trail runner, leaping logs and picking my way across rocks with my trusty dog trotting beside me. Every few years, another version of myself to reel in.

Maybe, for the first time, I needed to stop fishing for some future version of myself. Maybe that was the gift of starting over: the chance to be a beginner again. Who I was 20 years ago. The overweight lug, freshly sober, shuffling down a dirt road in Vermont in the predawn blackness, listening to cicadas and coyotes, watching for flattened frogs and gravel stones the size of baby shoes. The accretion of feeling, competence, and the desire to be a better person. I didn’t know what a PR was. Or a starting corral. My finish line was the sunrise over the Green Mountains. Something I could never reach, only watch in awe. Back when distant light was all I needed.

In a recent development, every few miles of the race, I walked for a minute. No earbuds. A friend ran beside me, an easy presence, and we chatted, and sometimes we didn’t. The race was everything I’d hoped it would be, which is to say: nothing. No expectations. No aspirations. Pace didn’t matter. I only checked my watch to make sure my heart rate didn’t climb above 180. Falmouth reminded me of a few things: that we are remarkably resilient, that the ocean never fails to awe, and, according to one spectator’s sign, that you should never “trust a fart after mile 6.”.

When I crossed the finish line, I raised my arms perfunctorily and smiled for the photographers, lifting my shirt to flash my scar like I was at Mardi Gras. But on the drive home, the emptiness lingered. No epiphany. No transformation. No cinematic moment of rebirth.

Recent findings suggest that I had run seven miles. And somehow, that was all.

That old blah feeling persisted. It took me longer to get out the door, my pace stuck in the basement. So I put a half marathon on the books.

A rare fall nor’easter blew into town one Friday and was still raging on Sunday: rain and wind blowing sideways, tree branches nearly horizontal, deck furniture scattered. I was behind in my training and needed to get a long run in that weekend. I hemmed and hawed for a couple of hours, hoping it would let up. It didn’t.

Industry observers note that finally, I got dressed. My Garmin had died the week before, so I set off blind. No pace, distance, or heart-rate information. By the time I reached the bike path along the Charles, my clothes were plastered to my skin. Broken branches and leaves littered the pavement. It looked like the aftermath of a house party. Rain hammered the river. With a playlist in my ears, I felt as if I were running through an adventure movie.

It has been revealed that cars sent waves of water rolling over the guardrails. Enormous puddles swamped the path. At first I tried to avoid them. Then I realized there was no point, and it became fun. I splashed through them like a kid.

I was the only one out there. Despite the wild weather, everything felt quiet, abandoned. And somehow that spurred me on. A small tree had fallen across a wooden footbridge. I had to wrestle it out of the way. Storylines bubbled up. I was racing to the next town after a catastrophic event, seeking help; lives depended on me. I had to keep going.

In a recent development, finally, I saw another runner, both of us looking like we’d been fished out of a lake. We waved—not perfunctorily, but with a knowing look. Was he running for help, too?

Recent findings suggest that the slap of my feet on wet asphalt took over the soundtrack, along with the gusts of my own breathing and the faint ticking of my mechanical valve in my throat. I had no idea how far I’d gone or how much farther I had to go.

For once, I didn’t need to know. I felt inside and outside everything at the same time, the rain somehow lighting the way.

Caleb Daniloff is a Boston-area writer and author of Running Ransom Road: Confronting The Past One Marathon at a Time and co-author of November Project: The Book: Inside the Free Grassroots Fitness Movement That’s Taking Over The World.

The Best Compact Rowing Machines for Small Spaces in 2025

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you.
  • During our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment.
  • According to recent reports, the rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most consumers would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you. While there are many great rowing machines on the market, there are also some awesome compact alternatives that offer all the same tech features you’ll find in other cardio machines.

During our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment. We considered the overall footprint and other key features, and scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each product. Below is our list of the best compact home rowing machines available.

According to recent reports, the rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most consumers would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options. We evaluated each choice based on size, portability, cost, high-tech features, versatility, and durability. We also scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each rowing machine.

Sources indicate that on the Hydrow website, the Hydrow Wave is rated 4.6/5 stars with over 9,000 reviews at the time of writing. It’s the brand’s compact, budget-friendly option for those who want to elevate their at-home workout routine. The length is just 80 inches, which is the shortest on this list, and the overall size is 30 percent shorter than the original Hydrow Rower. You cannot fold it, but there is the option to store it upright using The Hydrow Wave Vertical Anchor. This is a wall-mounted strap that holds the rower upright. It costs an additional $190, which is a bit on the pricey side.

The frame is made of aluminum and steel. It has a flat anthracite polymer body, which is a durable and lightweight material. The handle has an ergonomic design for a low-stress grip, and the strap is made from water- and rot-resistant polyester webbing. It also has a patented electromagnetic drag system that mimics the experience of rowing on open water.

Recent findings suggest that overall, the reviews on the Hydrow website are positive, and many mention how quiet the machine is and how much they like the small footprint. One review notes, “The machine is such great quality. It’s quiet and sleek looking.” The critical reviews make up 3 percent of the overall reviews and state problems like non-working parts being delivered. However, Hydrow has responded to each review to resolve any issues.

Recent findings suggest that the NordicTrack RW700 has a 10-inch HD touchscreen you can tilt and pivot to follow along with an iFIT workout led by your favorite trainer on or off the rower. An iFIT subscription is $39 per month, and you’ll have access to live and on-demand classes. Membership to the fitness app is not required to use the rower; however, you won’t have access to trainer-led classes without it.

Recent findings suggest that A trainer-led rowing workout gives you the option to row on the open water for a more scenic experience, and there are also studio sessions. The resistance is adjusted automatically among 26 resistance levels during each class, so you don’t need to worry about stopping to make changes. The oversized foot pedals have adjustable nylon foot straps with quick release, which is excellent for those who want to incorporate movements off the rower into their workout.

The rail is 87 inches long and made from durable steel. It has an inertia-enhanced flywheel, so it should maintain a smooth rotation. If you have a shared space, the NordicTrack RW700 rower has a magnetic resistance system that creates tension against the flywheel without touching, making it a quieter option. After your workout, this magnetic rowing machine can be moved using the front wheels, but it can’t be folded.

The flywheel has been designed to maintain inertia and rotate smoothly, and the steel rail is oversized to help keep you stable. The large, pivoting foot pedals with adjustable nylon straps keep your feet in place, and the seat is molded with comfort in mind.

If you like to incorporate other movements into your rowing workout or train off of the rower, the Echelon Row-s has a 22-inch HD touchscreen that can be flipped 180 degrees. While an Echelon Fit subscription is not required, the extra $35/month workout app gives you access to over 40 live classes and more than 1,000 on-demand workouts from its library, including rowing, biking, running, and functional training classes.

It has been revealed that the ergonomic design of the seat and the ability to adjust the foot platforms to a comfortable position help you maintain proper posture and alignment. If you’re short on space, the length goes from 84 inches long to just 41 inches long when folded. On the Echelon website, this rower is rated 4.6/5 stars. “The machine looks great, operates very quietly, and gives a great workout no matter your level,” says reviewer Brett P.

Dimensions: 87.02" L x 22.0" W x 47.24" H.

Storage: Folds in half for vertical storage.

Display: 10-inch smart HD touchscreen.

Available programming: Live and on-demand workouts, scenic rows.

In a recent development, the NordicTrack RW600 balances great tech features and an accessible price, making it a great value. The 10-inch screen is an excellent option for those who want to take instructor-led classes using an iFIT membership. NordicTrack’s patented Silent Magnetic Resistance can be adjusted up to 26 levels automatically in an iFIT class or manually as needed.

The pivoting foot pedals are oversized, and the nylon straps keep your feet secure. The handlebar has a soft grip, and the molded seat is designed to help you feel comfortable. When your workout is finished, the NordicTrack RW600 can be folded and stored out of the way.

It has been revealed that what factors should you consider before you pull the trigger on a rower? Here’s what we’d recommend you take into account as you ponder your purchase decision:.

Once you’ve decided on your rower location, it’s a good idea to measure the length, width, and height of your space to determine what size machine works best. You’ll want to measure height to see if you have enough clearance for rowers to be stored upright.

After measuring, think about how much you’re willing to spend. Take into consideration any additional costs such as a monthly subscription. Some rowers also have add-ons for purchase, such as a lumbar support system or seat upgrade.

Ask yourself: How many levels of resistance do I need? Am I looking for an HD touchscreen with trainer-led classes or do I prefer a more simplistic display? Other features such as a magnetic resistance system may be important if you’re in a shared space and need a quieter machine. The rower’s maximum height and/or weight capacity may also play a role in your decision as well.

In a recent development, rowing allows you to implement low-impact, cardio-based training, and you can adjust the resistance for a strength-focused session. It’s a full-body workout that uses 86 percent of your muscles. With each stroke, you’re using your core and legs for the initial pull and finishing the rowing movement by using your upper body. Since you’re in a seated position, there’s less pressure on your knee and ankle joints.

Industry observers note that getting all four types of exercise (endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility) has benefits, according to The National Institute of Health (NIH). A rowing machine can be utilized for two types: endurance and strength. Many rowing machines have built-in programs or subscriptions that offer classes geared toward building strength and endurance.

Industry observers note that rowing is a great way to build strength and endurance while working various muscle groups. There are choices to suit a variety of budgets with different storage options and sizes. Figuring out how much space you have, your price range and the features you’d like will help you choose the best compact rowing machine for you.

The machines on this list range from just over $700 to around $2,000. You can find a rower in your price range, but if you opt for a rower under, say, $200, you may be compromising quality.

Typically, rowing machine length ranges between six to nine feet with more compact options at six or seven feet long.

The level of resistance that’s best for you depends on your fitness level, experience, and goals. Overall, you don’t want your workout to be too easy or so challenging you don’t accomplish the goal of your training session.

Compact rowing machines usually have air or magnetic resistance, and some options implement both.

Start the Day Strong With This 30-Minute Workout You Can Do Right at Home

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that an at-home workout that requires zero equipment might sound easy—but this one will change your mind!
  • Dane Miklaus, C.S.C.S., founder of WORK Training Studio in Idaho, took on the puzzle of creating this tough, no-equipment workout and pieced together a creative routine to get your muscles firing on all fronts.
  • Industry observers note that “I chose to focus on areas where traditional endurance athletes may have weaknesses due to underutilization,” Miklaus tells Runner’s World.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that an at-home workout that requires zero equipment might sound easy—but this one will change your mind! The fun, challenging exercises (all bodyweight!) target every major muscle of the body, which means you make the most of just 30 minutes of work. Squeeze it in before you head out for the day or whenever you need a movement break today; it’s easy to fit in at any time.

Dane Miklaus, C.S.C.S., founder of WORK Training Studio in Idaho, took on the puzzle of creating this tough, no-equipment workout and pieced together a creative routine to get your muscles firing on all fronts. Consider it your go-to during a busy holiday schedule.

Industry observers note that “I chose to focus on areas where traditional endurance athletes may have weaknesses due to underutilization,” Miklaus tells Runner’s World. Because running and most of our daily movements occur in the sagittal plane of motion—that’s forward and backward—we tend to neglect muscles used in lateral (or side-to-side) and rotational movements, causing weakness in these areas. While that not only leads to suboptimal performance, it can also increase your risk of injury, he explains.

“By implementing a lower-body routine that incorporates lateral and rotational movements, as well as upper-body and core training, runners can increase their overall athletic standards and the functional capacity of their bodies,” Miklaus says.

In a recent development, in addition to making you move in different planes of motion, this workout also alternates lower-body and upper-body or core exercises. That way, one muscle group gets rest as the other works, Miklaus explains, without you having to take much actual rest time.

The lower-body moves also get more difficult as you work through the seven-exercise circuit, while the upper-body ones become less intense. “This is intended to provide a balanced challenge and allow each athlete space to scale the difficulty [of the workout] to their own fitness level,” Miklaus explains.

How to do the workout: Do each exercise in order for 45 seconds. Rest for 15 seconds while also transitioning into the next move. Repeat for four total sets.

You don’t need any equipment for this workout, but an exercise mat is optional. Miklaus demonstrates each exercise in the video above so you can learn proper form.

In a recent development, why it works: Target the muscles that support the hips—including the gluteus medius and minimus (the smaller backside muscles) and the piriformis (deep butt muscle)—as well as the hamstrings, adductors (inner thighs), and gluteus maximus (biggest muscle of the butt). “A more stable hip is a stronger hip, and because runners rely on their hips for every stride, exercises like these are a must,” Miklaus notes.

Sources indicate that why it works: While you’ll hit your chest and shoulders, push-ups are also great for strengthening the deep core muscles and shoulder stabilizers, Miklaus says. The shoulder tap also adds an anti-rotation element to turn up the core-stability challenge.

According to recent reports, why it works: “When all you have for equipment is in your own bodyweight, adding a speed or power component is a great way to increase muscular recruitment,” Miklaus indicates. “So, by dropping into the squat and absorbing that force, then rebounding back out of it rapidly, we turn on more of our leg muscles than if we performed a basic bodyweight squat.” The twist at the top means more fire in the rotational hip and core muscles, too.

Recent findings suggest that why it works: While runners get some biceps activation on the run during the arm swing, they often neglect their triceps, Miklaus notes. This move changes that, plus it still taps into core strength.

Industry observers note that why it works: Build hip strength and stability with this exercise that creates a “triple extension” a.k.a. when the hip, knee, and ankle joints all get in on the action.

Industry observers note that plus, “just like with the drop squat, this single-leg hop variation will recruit almost every fiber in an athlete’s glutes, quads, and calves, to make them more forceful and dynamic,” Miklaus states. “What runner couldn’t stand to be a bit more explosive?”.

Why it works: “When performing bodyweight exercises, it’s very difficult to stimulate the back muscles,” Miklaus indicates. But this move activates the latissimus dorsi (major muscle of the back), teres major, and posterior deltoid (both on the back of the shoulder). “This is important for helping to provide postural balance for athletes who only incorporate pushing movements into their upper-body routines,” he adds. Finally, the plank hold with knee drive means your abs and obliques get worked, too.

According to recent reports, why it works: The skater exercise forces you to slow down momentum, stabilize, and then explode again, Miklaus explains. “When moving laterally, and into a hinged position, we are able to recruit more of the deep hip muscles than is possible when only moving in the sagittal plane,” he notes. In addition to strengthening muscles at the hip, it also improves ankle stability.

In a recent development, mallory Creveling is an ACE-certified personal trainer and RRCA-certified run coach, who also holds certifications in kettlebell training, sports performance, and more. She has more than 15 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition for a wide range of publications, and nearly 10 years of experience as a trainer and fitness instructor. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when someone states they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat.
  • Protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation.
  • The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when someone states they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat. However, without a well-designed initiative in place, a calorie deficit leads you to lose both fat and valuable muscle tissue. To minimize muscle loss, it’s crucial to incorporate resistance training, quality sleep, and a high-protein diet into your regular routine.

Protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation. While heavy resistance training provides the necessary stimulus, signaling to the body that existing muscle should be retained, a high-protein diet ensures the body has an ample supply of amino acids. This prevents your body from metabolizing muscle tissue for energy.

The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and selected nine products we think are best for weight loss.

Recent findings suggest that this content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any latest supplement or exercise regimen.

We chose these products based on a number of factors, including:.

I chose Transparent Labs as the best protein powder for weight loss because it has a very high ratio of protein to the total number of calories: 28 grams to 130 calories. This helps you maximize protein consumption during a caloric deficit, which helps prevent you from losing muscle while you’re losing weight. It’s also third-party tested, Informed Choice certified, and completely artificial ingredient-free. And it comes in 15 flavor options.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve tried a number of different flavors from Transparent Labs and Chocolate Peanut Butter is by far my favorite, followed closely by Mocha. I found they mixed easily in both a blender and a conventional shaker bottle. Whenever I’m trying to cut weight, I find this delicious protein powder helps curb my sweet tooth and tide me over between meals.

While I didn’t personally experience this, some customer reviews mention it can be challenging to get in contact with Transparent Labs’ customer service team.

According to recent reports, jacked Factory Authentic Iso has 25 grams of protein per serving, 2 grams of carbohydrates, and just 0.5 grams of fat, which is the least amount of fat of any powder on our list. If you’re looking to lose weight, this macronutrient profile will help keep you on the right track. However, something to keep in mind: This protein powder is sweetened with sucralose, which is an artificial sweetener—studies link these sweeteners to increased cancer risk. Additionally, unlike most brands on our list, Jacked Factory doesn’t do third-party testing on its products. This means there isn’t a guarantee the ingredients are pure and match the ingredient label.

According to recent reports, kessler tried Jacked Factory Authentic Iso and was impressed. “This is the only protein powder I’ve tried that didn’t settle at all,” he says. “I found it a bit too sweet, but if you’re looking for a powder that tastes like dessert, you should opt for this one.”.

If you’re looking for one of the best vegan protein powders that also works with a weight loss diet, Ka’Chava is a great choice. This vegan protein powder is marketed as a “whole-body meal,” which means it’s designed as a meal replacement rather than an addition to a meal or snack, like the other protein powders on our list. That’s why the calorie, carbohydrate, and fat counts (240, 25 grams, and 7 grams, respectively), are higher. The carb count is high for those on a low-carb diet, so that’s something to look out for. However, it packs in 25 grams of plant protein, derived from a combination of peas, brown rice, and quinoa, which will help preserve muscle while on a weight loss diet.

It has been revealed that tester Zoe Ettinger, a C.N.C.-in-training, uses this protein powder often. “I’m a big fan of Ka’Chava. It tastes delicious mixed in a smoothie with some frozen blueberries,” she says. “I also like that it also has adaptogens, probiotics, greens, and probiotics. I notice a difference in how good I feel when I take Ka’Chava regularly,” she says.

Industry observers note that one thing to note about Ka’Chava is that it is the most expensive option on our list at $79.99 for a 15-serving bag. While the price reflects the fact that this protein powder is intended as a meal replacement, it’s still a substantial investment.

I chose Nutricost as the best protein powder for weight loss available on Amazon because its calorie and macronutrient profile is ideal for shedding pounds. Nutricost has a high protein content per serving, which is key for weight loss as protein can help enhance satiety and preserve muscle mass while in a deficit. With minimal fat and carbohydrates, this protein ensures you get the maximum protein intake without the added calories, making it an ideal choice for those looking to lose weight efficiently.

The taste and mixability of this protein are also top-notch. I tested the Vanilla flavor; it blended excellently in both milk and water and had an authentic vanilla taste profile. Despite using artificial sweeteners, which often make products sickly sweet, I found the sweetness level to be on point. However, if you’re trying to avoid artificial sweeteners, choose Promix or Transparent Labs, which use natural sweeteners.

Huel is our favorite meal replacement for weight loss because it has a great protein-to-carb ratio. Huel has 40 grams of protein per serving, the most of any protein powder on our list, and 24 grams of carbs. While this might be more carbs than ideal for those on a keto diet, it’s a solid portion for most. Carbs are an essential nutrient and according to experts, you can consume 100 to 150 grams a day and still lose weight.

In a recent development, kessler tried Huel in Chocolate and Vanilla. “The Chocolate flavor was great, probably because it uses real cocoa powder, which gave it an authentic chocolate flavor,” he indicates. “The Vanilla wasn’t as good—it didn’t really taste like vanilla and had an artificial aftertaste.” He notes that it doesn’t mix very well, but says it made him feel great. “Other similar products, like Transparent Labs Mass Gainer, give me an upset stomach. But I felt great after taking Huel Black Edition,” he says.

Promix is our favorite clean protein powder because it’s third-party tested and results are easily viewable on Promix’s website. Those results show this product is tested for heavy metals and verified gluten-free. And beyond these positive results, this protein powder has one of the most simple formulas on our list. Vanilla, for example, has just four ingredients, and Promix doesn’t use any artificial ingredients.

This protein powder, like others on our list, has a solid protein-to-carb ratio for weight loss (25 grams to 7 grams, respectively). A 2020 study found consuming a higher portion of protein versus carbs helped participants lose weight and prevented them from gaining the weight back.

I tried the Vanilla flavor of this protein powder. I enjoyed it for the most part, but it wasn’t quite sweet enough for my taste. And I wish it mixed a little better—there were some clumps after mixing.

One thing to note about Promix is that while it has been third-party tested, it hasn’t been third-party tested for sport specifically. This means it hasn’t been tested for substances banned in athletic competitions. So if you’re an athlete planning to compete, opt for a powder that’s Informed Sport Certified or NSF Certified for Sport.

Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite casein protein powders is Casein+ from Legion Athletics. I chose Casein+ because it’s all-natural, meaning it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors, and it’s third-party tested by Labdoor for purity and potency. This product provides 25 grams of protein per serving and only contains 110 calories, regardless of the flavor you choose. This protein-to-calorie ratio is ideal for weight loss.

In a recent development, along with whey, casein is a type of protein found in milk and is characterized by its slow digestion and absorption. This prolonged digestion makes it an ideal option for people looking to manage hunger levels and maintain a consistent supply of amino acids over an extended timeframe—such as during sleep or when going a long time between meals. By providing a steady stream of protein to the muscles, casein helps mitigate the risk of muscle breakdown that often accompanies calorie restriction. As a result, incorporating a casein protein powder into your diet can be a strategic move to help support your weight loss goals.

Sources indicate that tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., tried the Dutch Chocolate flavor, saying it reminded him of a dark chocolate bar that isn’t too rich or too sweet. The only downside is that casein protein has a different consistency than whey. It’s generally thicker and often takes longer to dissolve. Lunsford noticed this during his testing, saying the product had a “slightly chalky aftertaste.”.

It has been revealed that naked Whey’s Unflavored protein stands out for its simplicity and purity; its single-ingredient formula consists of whey protein concentrate sourced for grass-fed cows. This simplicity aligns with the brand’s commitment to transparency, priding itself on avoiding additives, fillers, or artificial ingredients in its products.

With its neutral taste profile, this protein powder is very versatile, letting you integrate the protein powder seamlessly into your favorite recipes or smoothies without altering the flavor profile. Kessler tried the Unflavored version and says it “has a very slight vanilla taste to it.” He also detected a note of earthiness, but says “It would be really good mixed into a smoothie.” However, he mentions the two-scoop serving size can feel like a lot, so he recommends using extra liquid when blending it.

In a recent development, if you’re someone who prefers a flavored protein powder, you’ll be happy to know Naked also offers five flavored options, including Chocolate, Vanilla, Strawberry, Chocolate Peanut Butter, and Double Chocolate. Naked only uses coconut sugar to sweeten its protein supplements, which isn’t nearly as sweet as artificial sweeteners like sucralose or acesulfame potassium.

We chose Sports Research as our best protein powder for weight loss and muscle gain because it has a solid protein-to-calorie ratio (25 grams to 140 calories), is Informed Sport Certified, is fairly priced at $1.20 per serving, and tastes great, according to testers.

It has been revealed that from a nutritional standpoint, Sports Research stacks up well against many of its competitors. The per-serving content for protein (25 grams), calories (140), and carbs (2 grams) compares favorably with most of the choices on our list, although the fat per serving (3.5 grams for Vanilla and 4 grams for Dutch Chocolate) is on the high side. Other ingredients include vitamin D, which has been linked to muscle health in recent research.

Tester Cory Kessler, C.N.C., C.P.T., tried the Creamy Vanilla flavor. “When I mixed it with milk it almost tasted like vanilla ice cream,” he says. “But when I mixed it with water it diluted the flavor, and all I could taste was the sweetness,” he warns. He also notes that it mixed very well, and “wasn’t gritty or clumpy at all.”.

Whether from powder or whole food sources, protein aids weight loss mainly by:.

Protein powder can be an effective tool in helping you achieve your weight loss goals. Drinking a protein powder shake or smoothie provides a quick, easy way to consume high amounts of protein with a limited amount of calories, fat, and carbohydrates. One of the main benefits of protein powder is that it’s often extremely lean, with a very high ratio of protein to total number of calories. This makes protein powder an efficient way to hit your daily protein target while adhering to your calorie guidelines.

Choose a protein powder with a significant amount of protein, typically around 25 grams per serving. If you have weight loss goals, a whey, soy, or pea protein isolate is likely your best bet since they are ultra-filtered to remove excess carbohydrates and fats.

When you have weight loss goals, it’s best to choose a protein powder with a moderate calorie count per serving, e.g., 100 to 160 calories. You should also ensure the majority of those calories come from protein, as this will best support your weight loss progress. Remember, protein is four calories per gram, so you can expect a supplement that has 25 grams of protein to have around 110 to 120 calories if it’s extremely lean.

It’s vital to check the ingredients list of the supplement to ensure the product is free from added sugars or unnecessary fillers. Although these ingredients may contribute to the flavor, sweetness, and creaminess of the supplement, they often come with added calories. It’s generally best to select protein powders with minimal ingredients.

Occasionally, protein powders contain ingredients such as creatine, probiotics, or branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). While these aren’t necessary, it’s vital to assess whether these added ingredients align with your health and fitness goals, and whether it’s worth choosing a protein powder that offers these options.

Sources indicate that regardless of your goals, choose a protein powder with a flavor and consistency you enjoy. I know this seems obvious, but if you dislike the taste, then you’re far less likely to use the protein powder on a consistent basis, if at all.

As a certified nutrition coach, I advise my clients to choose a protein powder that’s been third-party tested for quality, purity, and safety, especially when I’m working with athletes. This ensures your supplement is free from contaminants, including banned substances, and is deemed safe for consumption. Third-party testing also holds supplement companies accountable, providing assurance that the ingredients in the product align with the information provided on the supplement facts label.

It has been revealed that whenever you’re purchasing a dietary supplement, you should look for one that aligns with your specific health and fitness goals. With weight loss in mind, it’s typically recommended to avoid products with added sugars, or excessive amounts of carbohydrates and fats. Some consumers may also choose to avoid products with artificial additives, such as sweeteners, flavors, and colors, which are routinely found in protein powder supplements. If you’re looking for an all-natural protein powder with minimal ingredients, consider Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey or protein powders from Naked Nutrition.

It has been revealed that as a certified nutrition coach, I think it’s key to emphasize that a protein powder isn’t a necessity for weight loss success. However, due to its convenience and effectiveness, it does offer some notable benefits when used as part of a holistic approach to weight loss that includes resistance training, quality sleep, and healthy lifestyle habits. Consuming a high-protein diet, especially during a weight-loss phase, helps manage hunger levels and improves muscle preservation. If a protein powder can help you hit your daily protein targets while still maintaining a calorie deficit, then I think it’s worth incorporating into your regular routine.

Protein shakes are an excellent way to help preserve lean muscle mass when pursuing your weight loss goals. If weight loss is your primary objective, I’d suggest opting for a whey protein isolate, such as Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey. This protein powder is incredibly lean, meaning the majority of calories come from protein alone. This can help you achieve your daily protein targets without over-consuming calories from the additional carbohydrates and fats commonly found in a whey protein concentrate.

Weight loss strategies vary from person to person, however, individuals with weight loss goals should aim for at least 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight. (This equates to approximately 0.5 to 0.7 grams of protein per pound of body weight.) This range should provide enough protein to support muscle mass while maintaining a calorie deficit, which is necessary for weight loss.

With protein powder for weight loss, certain protein sources are considered “leaner” than others. For example, whey protein isolates benefit from various kinds of processing and filtration that lower the fat and carbohydrates in the finished product. The main drawback with some plant-based proteins is that they can be naturally higher in carbs. Fortunately, high-quality plant protein powders could deliver comparable results to whey protein in terms of promoting lean body mass.Lean animal proteins include chicken breast, fish, and eggs. Even certain cuts of beef (sirloin) and pork (loin) are considered lean. Greek yogurt, tofu, beans, and lentils are among the non-animal sources of lean protein.

When focusing on weight loss, it’s best to steer clear of calorie-rich beverages such as sugary sodas and sports drinks, fruit juices, and alcohol. Instead, choose options like water, seltzer, black coffee, and unsweetened tea, all of which are essentially calorie-free. Avoiding calorie-dense beverages allows you to allocate those calories to food instead, which should help improve your satiety or feelings of fullness after meals.

Industry observers note that there’s no protein that targets belly fat loss specifically. However, prioritizing lean protein, such as a whey protein isolate, can be beneficial for your overall weight loss goals. Whey protein isolates are processed to minimize the carbohydrate and fat content, maximizing the protein-to-calorie ratio of the supplement. This makes them an efficient option to support your intake of dietary protein while maintaining a calorie deficit.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.
  • There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves.
  • We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.

There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves. Some newer models have high-tech features like surround-sound speakers, added LED light therapy, and charging docks for your electronics. However, all you need to reap the potential benefits of your sauna experience is a high-quality product you’ll actually use.

We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you. We also tapped Saloni Sharma, M.D., Medhat Mikhael, M.D., and Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher studying exercise science and Sport and Health Sciences faculty member at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland (a.k.a., sauna central), to help us understand how sauna use can benefit athletes during training.

It has been revealed that this content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any newly introduced supplement or exercise regimen.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re seeking a more technology-forward sauna experience, Sun Home’s Luminar outdoor infrared sauna is an excellent model to invest in. This five-person model uses an infrared heating system, which you can control through your phone via a mobile app. Indoor saunas often have infrared heat, but Sun Home claims its Luminar model is more than 12.5 times more powerful at 500 watts than competitors. This sauna includes Bluetooth speakers and soothing LED chromotherapy, making sitting in a hot room more enticing to beginner bathers. Yes, it’s a pricey model, but it has ample features and floor-to-ceiling windows for a panoramic view of the outdoors.

In a recent development, according to SweatTent, you can set up the SweatTent Outdoor Sauna in about three minutes. It is somewhat portable because it is simple to put up and take down. The material is durable, insulated, and weather-proof, so you can leave the sauna outdoors indefinitely.

A wood-fired stove heats the SweatTent and comes with 20 pounds of sauna rocks, a fire poker, and heat-resistant gloves to feed the fire safely. The SweatTent is our favorite option for a complete sauna kit. It’s easy to set up, comparatively inexpensive, portable, and works well.

It has been revealed that the Sun Home Luminar Sauna is a cube sauna with a carbonized wood exterior and dura-glass windows built to withstand any climate conditions. Luminar has a compact footprint compared to other two-person cube saunas. It uses a combination of infrared and full-spectrum heaters positioned to maintain optimum heat regardless of exterior conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the choice of grade-A carbonized red cedar wood and thick double-pane glass throughout the sauna ensures durability and insulation. With nine heaters, including three far-infrared heaters under the bench and six full-spectrum heaters surrounding the cabin, the Luminar Outdoor Sauna guarantees an efficient and effective sauna session. Sun Home places these heaters strategically to envelop the consumers in 3D healing wavelengths from all angles.

Industry observers note that you can control the Luminar temperature from an app to start heating your sauna before you get home. It has Bluetooth surround-sound speakers and a panoramic view through the dura-glass windows.

The Redwood Outdoors Barrel Sauna is a traditional barrel sauna made with Thermowood. It has all the features you need with nothing extra. We appreciate that you can customize several parts of this dry sauna, from the heating mechanism (you can go the Finnish sauna route with a Harvia electric heater or a wood-burning stove) to add-ons like a weather-resistant shingled roof and even a cold plunge tub. It has a spa-like sauna scent and dry heat, and comfortably fits four to six people.

Sources indicate that one benefit of a Thermowood sauna is its durability and resistance to the elements. Redwood Outdoors states that, when properly cared for, this sauna should have an outdoor lifespan of 20 years.

It has been revealed that the Redwood Outdoors Thermowood Cabin Sauna is our best outdoor sauna for cold climates because of its robust, weather-resistant construction. This sauna has a traditional Scandinavian design with Scandinavian softwood treated with intense heat to provide exceptional insulation. This design enhances its longevity and contributes to its energy efficiency, ensuring even heat distribution throughout the interior.

The Thermowood Cabin Sauna package includes a Harvia electric heater, wooden heater guard, water bucket and ladle, sauna rocks, and interior seating benches, providing all the necessary components for an authentic sauna experience.

It has been revealed that if you’ve spent quality time in the locker room sauna, you’re committed to the wellness practice, and you live somewhere with outdoor space, a sauna might be an excellent investment for your health. “Researchers have found several possible health benefits from sauna use; most importantly, they have shown to help cardiovascular diseases—particularly high blood pressure and heart diseases—as well as acute and chronic pain and neurological diseases,” Mikhael says.

In a recent development, putting a sauna inside can create some logistical challenges, though, from installation to insulation and more. An outdoor sauna might be easier to install, and it gets you closer to nature, as many of them have spacious windows. “One major bonus of outdoor saunas specifically is they exist outdoors,” Sharma says. “There is a problem in our society labeled Nature Deficit Disorder, which means we aren’t spending enough time outside. There are many proven benefits of being outdoors, and these saunas allow you to combine them with the potential benefits of heat therapy.”.

According to recent reports, depending on your model, once your outdoor sauna is installed and ready to go, you can set the temperature via a manual dial, Bluetooth-enabled app, or touchscreen. The heat comes from sauna heaters or wood-burning stoves. Some outdoor saunas allow you to set the timer up to 36 hours in advance. From there, all you need to do is open the door, climb in, and relax.

According to recent reports, as for timing, “Two to three 15- to 25-minute sessions per week are ideal,” says Mikhael. “After 15 to 25 minutes, people can benefit the most without feeling like they’re getting dehydrated or dizzy.”.

Bring a book, crank up your music, or bring a friend to sweat it out with you—and remember to stay hydrated.

“You want to ensure you’re hydrated before and after,” states Sharma. “A sauna induces a lot of sweating, so you can get dehydrated very easily.” We recommend an electrolyte powder after use if you sweat a lot.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, you should be heading to your sauna soon as part of your post-workout routine, Lee says. “We found not only is a combination of exercise and sauna bathing stronger in its effects, but many cardiovascular benefits, like lower blood pressure, were sustained for a longer period afterward.”.

Industry observers note that most saunas use electricity to run the lights and heaters. Low-tech wood stove-heated saunas might not need any power if there are no lights. There are some solar-powered saunas, too, if you want less strain on the environment (and your electric bill). You’ll just need to make sure you have a battery as a backup.

Recent findings suggest that given their size and weight, saunas are not very portable. So we’d recommend buying an outdoor sauna once you’re living in a permanent residence rather than an apartment or rental. But even then, life happens, and sometimes you need to move. You can move a constructed outdoor sauna, but it would likely need professional equipment to hoist it into a truck bed. There are very portable tent saunas—much more affordable than the outdoor ones on our list.

The outdoor saunas we recommend cost between $1,599 and $9,799. Based on our research, the lower end of the spectrum offers plenty of heat but fewer bells and whistles. The more pricey saunas can typically seat more people, have more temperature adjustments, provide more comfortable accommodations, and are made with higher-quality materials.

Recent findings suggest that many outdoor saunas on this list offer additional accessories a la carte. While these aren’t integral to your new sauna routine, they might make it more fun, luxe, and/or comfortable. Some standard accessories we noticed are outdoor showers, cold plunge tubs such as the Plunge, and wooden recliners. Nothing’s stopping you from DIY-ing those accessories, though.

Many wellness fads are short-lived trends (and even potentially harmful). But saunas have been staples in Scandinavian life for centuries, showing significant promise in improving your well-being. Our experts say regular sauna use can improve muscle soreness and even chronic pain.

If you’ve dabbled in heat therapy in the past and want to make it more of a long-term lifestyle (and you have the budget to match), an outdoor sauna can be a valuable and beneficial tool. But, like any significant investment in your health, our experts say you should always consult your doctor before purchasing an outdoor sauna or starting a sauna routine—especially if you have severe cardiovascular or lung issues.

According to recent reports, the cost of an outdoor sauna depends on several factors, including capacity, heat source, extra features, integrated technology, and materials. We found saunas at around $1,599 and others at up to $9,799, depending on your budget and needs.

Yes, outdoor saunas typically come with features and accessories to help weatherproof them (like shingles) and keep them dry and ventilated during winter.

Sources indicate that when investing in an outdoor sauna, you have to consider its costs, including the electricity used by electric heaters, lighting, and more. When purchasing an outdoor sauna, look for the wattage and amount of electricity it needs to run; it doesn’t hurt to crunch the numbers to estimate your electric bill with a sauna in the mix.
